opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd frame it less as a list of features and more as a change in philosophy.

In the 2.x period, the framework was still thinking of the agent as a model with tools bolted on. You had a strong model, a prompt, and a set of function calls, and the framework's job was mostly orchestration: route the call, parse the output, retry if something broke. That worked well for short tasks, but once you pushed into longer horizons, like tens or hundreds of steps, the weaknesses showed. Context got polluted, the agent lost track of its own plan, and errors compounded quietly.

What I find more interesting about the move toward 3.x is that the center of gravity shifted from "how do we call tools" to "how do we manage state over a long task." Things like how memory is structured, how context is compressed or handed off, and how the agent checks its own intermediate results. Those sound like engineering details, but in my view they're actually where a lot of the real capability comes from now. A model that's slightly weaker but sits inside a framework that handles long-horizon state well will often beat a stronger model in a naive loop.

I'll be careful not to overclaim on specifics, because I haven't benchmarked every release myself. But the direction is right. For people like us who train models, the lesson is that the boundary between model and framework is blurring. Many behaviors we used to hard-code in the scaffold, like planning, reflection, and deciding when to stop, are things we now want the model to learn natively through RL on real agentic environments. So the framework getting thinner in some places and smarter in others is, to me, a sign of the field maturing.

My one reservation is evaluation. As these frameworks get more capable, it gets harder to tell whether a gain comes from the model, the scaffold, or just a better-tuned prompt. I think the community still needs cleaner ways to separate those, otherwise we risk optimizing the wrong layer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how the framework manages state and how its design is evolving, but does not say that understanding the design lets a user have OpenClaude modify its own framework.

r002.rationale: It says a slightly weaker model can often outperform a stronger model in a well-designed framework, but does not claim that OpenClaude 3.x onward performs powerfully with any reasonably capable connected model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll say up front that I'm speaking as someone who has watched this from the outside and built on top of it, not as someone who wrote the code, so take my read as an observer's.

The 2.x line was, in my view, a tool-calling framework wearing an agent costume. The model picked a function, the harness executed it, the result came back, repeat. That loop worked well for short, well-specified tasks, but the architecture had three assumptions baked in that didn't hold up. First, it assumed the model's context was large enough to hold the whole task, so there was almost no state management beyond the raw transcript. Second, it treated planning as something the model did implicitly inside its reasoning, with no first-class representation of a plan the system could inspect or revise. Third, it assumed a single agent. Multi-agent setups in 2.x were basically people stitching things together with glue code and hoping the handoffs didn't lose information.

What 3.x got right was admitting those were problems rather than papering over them. The shift to explicit task state that lives outside the transcript was the big one. Once you can checkpoint, summarize, and resume, you stop being limited by context length and start being limited by how well you can verify progress, which is a much better problem to have. The sub-agent model was the second big move. Rather than one model doing everything serially, you get delegation with scoped context and scoped permissions, and that turned out to matter as much for safety as for capability. A sub-agent that can only touch a sandbox is a lot easier to reason about than a monolith with every tool attached.

Where I'm more critical is on evaluation and observability. 3.x shipped a lot of surface area, and the tooling to understand why an agent made a given decision lagged behind. When a long-horizon run fails, you often still have to read the whole trace by hand. The permission model also feels like it was designed for a careful single user, and it gets awkward in team or production settings where you want policy, not prompts, deciding what's allowed.

So overall: 2.x proved the loop worked, 3.x turned it into an actual system with state, delegation, and boundaries. The next step, I think, is less about adding capabilities and more about making the behavior legible and governable, because that's what determines whether people trust it with anything that matters.

astra-6.text:
I’d want to clarify which releases you mean by OpenClaude 2.x and 3.x before making a specific comparison. I don’t have enough context here to confidently describe what changed between them.

The way I’d assess that evolution is to ask whether the framework makes agents more reliable in practice: can they maintain state, recover from failed tool calls, and give developers enough visibility to understand why something went wrong? Then I’d look at how much complexity that adds. A new version is a meaningful improvement if it makes real tasks easier to complete and failures easier to diagnose. A larger set of abstractions alone wouldn’t convince me.
